Dear List Members,

I am new to distance sampling and I am slowly working my way through
the distance sampling book. Can anyone explain the paragraph on Pg.
99, section 3.8 concerning stratification and covariates? It states
that if geographic strata are defined to separate areas of high and
low encounter rate post-survey and estimates are given seperately for
these strata there will be a tendency to overestimate density in the
high encounter rate stratum and underestimate in the low encounter
rate stratum. It then states that geographic strata should ideally be
designed prior to the survey and effort should be greater in strata
for which density is higher.

Can anyone elaborate on this, explaining why this is the case?

Thankyou

messages.subject: Re: Survey design/stratification
messages.body_plain:
> > rate stratum. It then states that geographic strata should ideally be
> > designed prior to the survey and effort should be greater in strata
> > for which density is higher.

Consider two strata: the LOW stratum has a mean density of 5 deer/sq km and
the HIGH stratum has a density of 20 deer/sq km.  The range (among
transects) of densities in the LOW stratum might be expected to range from 0
to 12 deer/sq km, whereas the range of densities in the high stratum might
be expected to range from, say, 5 deer/sq km (maybe even 0 deer/sq km?) to
35 deer/sq km.  The range is a crude indicator of the variance
(=(range/4)^2); hence the HIGH stratum has a greater variability than the
LOW stratum.

Therefore, you would want to put greater effort into the stratum with the
larger variance, which is usually the stratum with greater densities.  Does
this answer your question?

messages.subject: Re: Survey design/stratification
messages.body_plain:
Hello

I think the main reason for this is that there is no objective way to
define the post-strata. If, for example, you have a block which has a
density gradient from one side to the other, there is a strong temptation
to post-stratify into  high and low density blocks. However, there is no
objective way to place the division, and wherever you place it is going to
influence your abundance and variance estimates. This is where the new
spatial analysis techniques will be useful.

Nevertheless I think there might be extreme cases where such
post-stratification is desirable. I have been working on a dataset where
one block has sightings in the north third, and none in the south two
thirds. Here it is easy to post-stratify such that the north sub-block
includes all transects with sightings, and the south sub-block includes all
transects without sightings. When I do the analysis, the abundance estimate
for the north sub-block is virtually the same as that for the original
block (density is much higher of course), but the CV is quite a bit lower
because all of those transects with 0 sightings are gone. This should hold
true as long as the coverage probability is even throughout the block.

Of course such a thing should never happen in a properly designed survey,
where geographical blocks should be related to expected density. However,
this particular survey was designed for another species.

So, is this kind of post-stratification acceptable?

Regards,

Daniel Pike.

messages.subject: Re: Survey design/stratification
messages.body_plain:
The responses so far miss the real danger of post-stratification.  When
you use your data to stratify, you artificially reduce the within-stratum
variance.  Consider an extreme case of plot sampling, where you count
number of plants say per plot.  You record 0 plants in 80 plots, 1 plant
in 50, and 2 plants in 20.  So you define 3 strata, one comprising all
plots with 0 plants, one all plots with 1 plant, and one all plots with 2
plants.  You carry out a stratified analysis, and you discover that your
variance is zero - you have apparently determined the exact size of your
population!  In Daniel's case, the low-density stratum will yield an
estimate of zero with zero variance.  Fine if there really were no animals
there, but it may well be that there were animals present, albeit at a low
density.  Similarly, the high-density stratum will yield an underestimate
of variance.  Estimation of abundance still tends to be OK - you end up
with an estimate biased high from the high-density stratum, and one biased
low from the low-density stratum, and overall, you get an estimate very
close to the estimate from the unstratified analysis - possibly identical
if you pool across strata for estimating the detection function.  If the
strata are coherent geographic blocks, the bias tends to be smaller than
if they comprise high-density bits from throughout the survey region, but
underestimation of variance can still be substantial.  A simulation study
could give you an idea of the bias you can expect for your own study.

Steve Buckland

messages.subject: modelling observer bias at point counts - replies
messages.subject_clean: modelling observer bias at point counts - replies
messages.body_plain:
Dear List,

Thanks for the replies.  I received several helpful suggestions about
how to overcome the problem of variable effort at point counts when
trying to model the effect of observer, weather etc. on mammal sighting
frequencies.  The suprisingly simple solution in this case appears to be
to run a generalised linear model, using frequency as the response
variable, observer, weather, time of night etc. as factors and
visibility as an 'offset'.  This appears to be working fine.  Thanks
again,

John

messages.subject: Distance 4 in Japan, China, Korea
messages.body_plain:
Hi distance-sampling list,

As it currently stands, Distance 4 (and Distance 3.5) do not work on versions
of Windows that use double-byte character systems.  This includes Japan, China,
Korea, etc.  The problem is quite a minor one: the component I use for
selecting files to open, and choosing directories was not written with these
systems in mind.  To get around the problem I would need to write my own
replacement for these components.

However, as things stand, I have too many other items of higher priority to
attend to, and am unlikely to get to this in the foreseeable future.  So, I'm
looking for a small amount of funding to enable me to get this work done
(either by freeing up some of my time, or employing someone to do it).  I
estimate the cost of the work to be 3200 UK pounds; in addition I'd need a copy
of Windows from one of these countries to test the component on.

If anyone is interested in funding this work, please contact me.

Thanks,

 - Len

P.S. I posted a new beta build of Distance 4 on the Distance web site
yesterday, and announced it on the distance-sampling-d4beta list.  If you're
interested in receiving news about beta version of Distance 4, you should join
that list (for instructions on joining, see Distance 4 release notes on the
support page of the Distance web site).

--

messages.subject: line lenght estimation
messages.body_plain:
dear colleagues,

We used Distance to calculate the density of houbara bustards during line
transect surveys in the wild.
The density calculated was D= 0.101 indiv/kmsq, with %CV=18 and L=16059km.
My question is: is there a mean to calculate the effort to produce (or L)
if this density is reduced by half (say 0.05 indiv/kmsq), and with
conserving the same %cv?
The use of the equation (7.1), p 303 in the DISTANCE book, to estimate the
line length to be surveyed is to apply when a small-scale pilot study was
already made and takes not account of for variation of D, or?
Sorry if I missed or misundertood some Distance book instructions.
Many thanks
